title: Illinois Rooms
bigQuestion: Who built the public fields, gyms and school leagues of Illinois, and who decided which neighborhoods and students could use them?

story.title: A Key on a School Night
story.kicker: A park-district worker unlocks a gym door, and a neighborhood walks in.
paragraphs: It is seven o'clock on a winter school night. A park-district worker turns a key in a steel door. The lights hum on over a wooden floor. Soon teenagers arrive for open gym, and a group of adults sets up for a league game.

The key belongs to a public body. In Illinois, a park district is its own unit of local government. It can collect property taxes, own land and hire staff. In Chicago, one park district has run the city's parks since 1934. In hundreds of other Illinois towns, voters elect park board members.

The same building may be shared with a school. On weekday mornings the gym holds physical education classes. On Friday nights it may hold a high school game played under the rules of the Illinois High School Association, founded in 1900. Two public institutions use one room.

Every such room has a history. Someone set aside the land. Someone voted for the tax. Someone decided which neighborhoods got a field house first. Sometimes people were kept out of a beach or a park by threats and custom. The history of Illinois sport is partly a history of keys and who held them.
story.think: Who do you think should decide where a new public gym gets built? Why?

lessons.title: Section Sixteen
lessons.mainIdea: The Land Ordinance of 1785 set aside one section of every township for public schools, tying land and schooling together in Illinois.
reading: In 1785 Congress passed the *Land Ordinance*. It set a plan to survey land west of the original states into square *townships*, each six miles on a side. Each township was cut into 36 sections of one square mile. Illinois land was later surveyed on this grid.

The ordinance reserved section 16 of every township for public schools. Towns could sell or rent that land and use the money for schools. Illinois became a state in 1818. Its early school funds came in part from these school lands.

This choice linked public land to public schooling from the start. Many later school buildings, playgrounds and athletic fields stand on land a public body owns for the public. When a school district builds a field, it follows that old idea that land can serve every child.

words.d: the 1785 law that set up the survey of western land into townships and sections
a square of land six miles on each side, divided into 36 sections
one square mile of land inside a township

look.title: Lot Sixteen for Schools
look.text: The ordinance reserved lot number 16 of every township for the maintenance of public schools within that township.
look.cite: Land Ordinance of 1785, Continental Congress, May 20, 1785
look.prompt: Why would a new nation set aside school land before towns even existed?

check.q: Which section of each township did the 1785 ordinance reserve for schools?
check.why: The Land Ordinance of 1785 reserved section, or lot, 16 for public schools.

check.q: How big is a township under the 1785 plan?
check.why: Each township was a square six miles on a side.

check.q: When did Illinois become a state?
check.why: Illinois became a state in 1818.

lessons.title: A Playground at Hull House
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1890s Hull House, a settlement house on Chicago's West Side, opened a playground and gym for crowded immigrant neighborhoods.
reading: In 1889 Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr opened *Hull House* on Halsted Street in Chicago. It was a *settlement house*, a center where reformers lived among working families and offered classes and services. The neighborhood was crowded with immigrants from Italy, Greece, Eastern Europe and other places.

Children there had few safe places to play. Streets were busy with wagons, and yards were small. In the 1890s Hull House opened a playground and a gymnasium. Its leaders argued that play space was a public need, like clean water or schools.

Reformers in Chicago and other cities formed a *playground movement*. They asked city governments, not only charities, to pay for play spaces. In 1906 the Playground Association of America was founded, with Jane Addams among its leaders. Their argument helped move play from private gifts to public budgets.

words.d: the settlement house opened in Chicago in 1889 by Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr
a neighborhood center where reformers lived and offered classes and services to working families
an early 1900s campaign to make cities build and pay for public play spaces

look.title: Who Pays for Play?
look.text: Plan A: a settlement house raises gifts from donors and opens one playground on its own lot. Plan B: the city passes a tax and opens playgrounds in many neighborhoods, run by public workers.
look.prompt: Which plan reaches more children? Which plan can voters change? Explain your thinking.

choices: Eunice Kennedy Shriver and Anne Burke
Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr

check.why: Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr opened Hull House on Halsted Street.

check.q: What did the playground movement ask cities to do?
choices: Build and pay for public play spaces
check.why: Reformers asked city governments to fund play spaces.

check.q: What is a settlement house?
choices: A neighborhood center where reformers lived and offered services
check.why: At a settlement house, reformers lived among working families and offered classes.

lessons.title: Field Houses of 1905
lessons.mainIdea: In 1905 Chicago's South Park Commission opened neighborhood parks with field houses, giving working families public gyms, pools and meeting rooms.
reading: Chicago once had many separate park boards. One was the South Park Commission. In the early 1900s, voters approved money for small neighborhood parks in crowded areas. The commission hired the Olmsted Brothers to design the parks. D. H. Burnham and Company designed the buildings.

In 1905 the first ten of these parks opened. Sherman Park, Davis Square and Armour Square were among them. Each had a *field house*. A field house held a gym, locker rooms and showers, a library branch and meeting rooms. Outdoors there were ball fields, a swimming pool and playgrounds.

The field house was a new kind of public room. It mixed sport, bathing, reading and clubs in one building. City leaders and visitors from other cities came to study the plan. President Theodore Roosevelt praised the small parks as a notable civic achievement.

words.d: a park building with a gym, showers, and meeting and reading rooms
one of Chicago's separate park boards before 1934, which built neighborhood parks on the South Side

look.title: Inside a Field House, 1905
look.text: Walk in the front door. On one side is a gymnasium with a wooden floor and a running track above it. On the other is an assembly hall. Upstairs there is a reading room run by the public library. Behind the building are showers, because many nearby homes had no bathtub.
look.prompt: Why would a park put showers and a library in the same building as a gym?

check.q: Which firm designed the landscapes of the 1905 South Side parks?
check.why: The Olmsted Brothers designed the parks; D. H. Burnham and Company designed the buildings.

check.q: What was inside a field house?
choices: A gym, showers, meeting rooms and a library branch
check.why: Field houses mixed a gym, showers, meeting rooms and reading rooms.

check.q: Which park opened in 1905 as one of the first ten?
check.why: Sherman Park was among the first ten neighborhood parks of 1905.

lessons.title: Twenty-Two Boards Become One
lessons.mainIdea: In 1934 Chicago's separate park boards were combined into the Chicago Park District, whose board the mayor appoints.
reading: By the early 1930s, Chicago had 22 separate park districts. Each had its own board, staff and taxes. The Great Depression left many of them short of money. Some could not pay their debts or keep parks open.

In 1934 voters approved combining them into one body, the *Chicago Park District*. The mayor appoints its board, with the approval of the City Council. The new district took over parks, beaches, field houses and pools across the city. It also received federal help through New Deal work programs, which built and repaired many park buildings.

The Park District also owns Soldier Field, the lakefront stadium that opened in 1924. It has hosted college football, the first Special Olympics games in 1968 and, since 1971, the Chicago Bears. A stadium owned by a park district is a public room, even when a private team uses it most.

words.d: the single public body formed in 1934 to run Chicago's parks, beaches and field houses
to combine several bodies into one
federal programs of the 1930s, under President Franklin Roosevelt, that put people to work on public projects

lessons.title: Park Boards Across Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: Outside Chicago, Illinois towns can form park districts with elected boards that tax, own land and run gyms and pools.
reading: Illinois law lets communities form *park districts*. A park district is a separate unit of local government, apart from the city and the school district. Voters in the area approve it. They then elect its board of *commissioners*.

A park district can levy a property tax, borrow money for buildings and buy land. It runs parks, pools, ice rinks, golf courses and recreation centers. Illinois has hundreds of park districts. Many suburbs and small towns have one.

Park districts and school districts often sign *joint-use agreements*. The school may use a district pool for swim meets. The park district may use a school gym for evening leagues. The agreement says who pays for staff, cleaning and repairs. Keys, schedules and insurance are all written down.

words.d: in Illinois, a separate local government that owns and runs parks and recreation
an elected or appointed member of a park district board
a written deal letting two public bodies share a building or field

look.title: One Gym, Two Owners' Rules
look.text: A school district owns a gym. The park district wants it for adult leagues on Tuesday and Thursday nights. The school wants the park district's pool for its swim team. The two boards meet to write one agreement.
look.prompt: List three things the agreement should say. Who should pay for the lights and cleaning?

check.q: Who elects park commissioners in most Illinois park districts?
check.why: Voters in the area elect the board of commissioners.

check.q: What can a park district do?
choices: Levy a property tax and own land
check.why: A park district can tax, borrow and buy land for parks.

check.q: What is a joint-use agreement?
choices: A written deal for two public bodies to share a place
check.why: It lets a school and a park district share a gym, pool or field.

lessons.title: The 1919 Beach
lessons.mainIdea: In July 1919 a Black teenager drowned after being stoned at an informally segregated Chicago beach, setting off a week of deadly violence.
reading: During and after World War I, many Black families moved from the South to Chicago. This was part of the *Great Migration*. They found jobs, but housing and public spaces were often split by race. There was no written law for Chicago beaches, but custom and threats drew lines.

On July 27, 1919, Eugene Williams, a Black teenager, was swimming off the beach near 29th Street. His raft drifted across the unmarked line. A white man threw rocks at him, and he drowned. A police officer refused to arrest the man. Fights broke out on the beach.

The violence spread across the city for about a week. Thirty-eight people died, 23 Black and 15 white, and hundreds were hurt. A state commission later studied the causes. Its 1922 report, The Negro in Chicago, pointed to housing, jobs and the unequal use of parks and beaches.

words.d: the movement of millions of Black Americans from the South to Northern and Western cities, beginning around 1915
keeping people apart by race, by law or by custom
a practice people follow by habit, even without a written law

look.title: The Commission Report of 1922
look.text: The commission found that fights over the use of parks, playgrounds and beaches had been a steady source of racial conflict in Chicago before the 1919 riot.
look.cite: Chicago Commission on Race Relations, The Negro in Chicago: A Study of Race Relations and a Race Riot, 1922
look.prompt: Why would a study of a riot look at parks and beaches?

check.q: What happened to Eugene Williams on July 27, 1919?
choices: He drowned after being stoned near 29th Street
check.why: A white man threw rocks at him after his raft crossed the unmarked line, and he drowned.

check.q: How was the line at the beach kept?
check.why: There was no written law; custom and threats drew the line.

check.q: What did the 1922 commission report find about parks?
choices: Parks had no role in the conflict
Fights over parks and beaches were a source of conflict
check.why: The Chicago Commission on Race Relations pointed to unequal use of parks and beaches.

lessons.title: Wade-Ins and a Court Decree
lessons.mainIdea: Protests at Rainbow Beach in 1960 and 1961 and a 1983 federal consent decree challenged unequal park use and spending in Chicago.
reading: Decades after 1919, some Chicago beaches still felt closed to Black residents. In 1960 and 1961, groups of Black and white protesters held *wade-ins* at Rainbow Beach on the South Side. They walked into the water together to claim the beach for everyone. They met angry crowds, and police were called to protect them.

Other gaps were about money. Parks in some neighborhoods got newer buildings, more programs and more staff than others. In 1983 the U.S. Department of Justice sued the Chicago Park District, saying Black and Latino neighborhoods received fewer services.

The case ended in a *consent decree*, a court-approved agreement. The Park District agreed to spread programs, staff and repairs more fairly across the city. A federal court watched over the agreement for years. Fairness now had to be measured and reported, not only promised.

words.d: a protest in which people enter a segregated beach or pool together
an agreement to settle a lawsuit that a court approves and enforces

look.title: Two Kinds of Unfair
look.text: Kind 1: a crowd threatens people who try to swim at a beach. Kind 2: a public body spends more on parks in some neighborhoods than in others. The wade-ins challenged the first kind. The 1983 lawsuit challenged the second.
look.prompt: Which kind is easier to see? Which is easier to prove with records? Explain.

choices: A protest where people entered a segregated beach together
check.why: Protesters walked into the water together to claim Rainbow Beach for everyone.

check.q: Who sued the Chicago Park District in 1983?
check.why: The Justice Department sued over unequal services to Black and Latino neighborhoods.

check.q: What is a consent decree?
choices: A settlement that a court approves and enforces
check.why: A consent decree is a court-approved agreement to end a lawsuit.

sections.title: The IHSA as a School Body

lessons.title: Principals Meet in 1900
lessons.mainIdea: The Illinois High School Association, founded in 1900, is an association of member schools that sets eligibility rules and runs state tournaments.
reading: In the late 1800s, high school teams often used players who were not really students. Some were older men or paid ringers. Schools argued over rules from game to game. Principals wanted schools, not outside clubs, to control school sport.

In 1900 Illinois principals founded the *Illinois High School Association*, or IHSA. Member schools agreed to follow shared rules on who could play. A player had to be an enrolled student making progress in classes. The IHSA's office is in Bloomington.

The IHSA is not a state agency. It is a private, not-for-profit association of member schools, both public and private. Today more than 800 high schools belong. It runs state series and championships in many boys and girls sports and in activities such as speech and music.

words.d: the association of Illinois high schools, founded in 1900, that sets eligibility rules and runs state tournaments
the rules that say who is allowed to play
a skilled outsider brought in to play as if he belonged to the team

look.title: Why Principals, Not Coaches?
look.text: Before 1900 a team captain or coach might recruit any strong player in town. After 1900 the IHSA required that players be enrolled students passing their classes, and member principals enforced the rule.
look.prompt: Why would principals want eligibility tied to classes? What does that say about what school sport is for?

check.q: When was the IHSA founded?
check.why: Illinois principals founded the IHSA in 1900.

choices: A private, not-for-profit association of member schools
check.why: The IHSA is an association of public and private member schools, not a state agency.

check.q: What problem did early eligibility rules address?
choices: Teams using players who were not really students

lessons.title: How a Bylaw Changes
lessons.mainIdea: IHSA member schools write and change their own bylaws through a yearly process that ends in a vote of member principals.
reading: The IHSA's rules are written in its *constitution* and *bylaws*. The constitution sets up the association and its board. Bylaws are the detailed rules, such as on eligibility, transfers and the number of contests allowed in a season.

Anyone at a member school can propose a change through the principal. Proposals go to town hall meetings held around the state each fall. A Legislative Commission of school representatives reviews them. Proposals it advances go on a ballot, and member school principals vote.

A separate *Board of Directors*, elected from school leaders, runs the association between votes. It hears appeals and hires the executive director. This design makes the IHSA a kind of small government. Its members are schools, and each school has a vote.

words.d: the founding rules that set up an organization and its leaders
the detailed rules an organization adopts under its constitution
the elected group of school leaders that runs the IHSA between votes

look.title: A Proposal's Path
look.text: Fall: a principal submits a proposal. Town hall meetings: schools discuss it in regions around the state. Winter: the Legislative Commission reviews it and sends some proposals to a ballot. Late winter: member principals vote. A rule that passes goes into the handbook.
look.prompt: At which stage could a school most easily change the wording of a proposal? Why?

check.q: Who votes on IHSA bylaw proposals?
check.why: Proposals that reach the ballot are voted on by member school principals.

check.q: What is the difference between a constitution and bylaws?
choices: Bylaws set up the board; the constitution lists game rules
The constitution sets up the body; bylaws are detailed rules
check.why: The constitution sets up the association; bylaws hold detailed rules like eligibility.

check.q: What does the IHSA Board of Directors do?
choices: Runs the association between votes and hears appeals
check.why: The elected board runs the IHSA day to day and hears appeals.

lessons.title: Championships Added Over Time
lessons.mainIdea: IHSA state championships were added one sport at a time, and the dates show when each group of students got a state title to play for.
reading: The IHSA did not start with every sport. It added state *championships* one by one. Boys tennis crowned its first state champion in 1912. Boys wrestling held its first state finals in 1937. Each new tournament meant new rules, officials and a place in the handbook.

Girls had to wait much longer. Most IHSA girls championships began in the 1970s, after Title IX became federal law in 1972. Some came much later. Girls wrestling held its first IHSA state finals in 2022, at the end of the 2021–22 season.

A championship is an *institution*, not just a game. It needs a bracket, seeding rules, host sites and paid officials. When the IHSA adds a sport, schools start teams because a state title now exists. The dates of first championships trace who was invited into school sport, and when.

words.d: an official contest that names a winner, such as a state title
an established organization or practice with rules that last over time
the set of regional, sectional and final rounds that leads to a state title

lessons.title: Required Gym Class
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois law has long required physical education in public schools, which is why nearly every school has a gym.
reading: Illinois law requires public schools to offer *physical education*. For many years the School Code called for daily physical education for students in kindergarten through grade 12. Illinois was known as one of the few states with such a broad daily rule. Later laws let some students be excused, such as students in certain sports or classes.

A rule for daily classes needs a room. That helps explain why Illinois school buildings from the 1900s onward nearly always include a gymnasium. Districts paid for gyms with local taxes and bonds approved by voters.

The gym built for classes then became the home of school teams and community events. Graduations, elections and assemblies were often held there. So one law about classes shaped the buildings in almost every Illinois town. It also gave park districts rooms to share after school.

words.d: school classes in movement, health and games
the Illinois law that sets rules for public schools
a way for a public body to borrow money, often approved by voters, to build things
